title: Coal, gas and petroleum projects should be excluded from the streamlined approval pathway and the national-interest exemption
oneLiner: The Greens' condition for passing the reforms, now law: the projects with the largest impacts keep the full assessment.
body: Under this proposal, adopted as part of the Labor–Greens deal on 28 November 2025, coal, gas and petroleum activities, including exploration, cannot use the streamlined assessment pathway, the national-interest exemption or bioregional planning approvals. The water trigger for large coal and unconventional gas projects stays with the Commonwealth rather than being devolved to states. The case for it is that these projects carry the largest and least reversible impacts, on land, water and climate, so speed should be denied to them first. The case against is that it puts gas supply projects, which the government's own energy plan and its reservation scheme rely on, into the slowest lane in the system.
contextBackground: This began as a Greens demand and became the price of passage. It is written here as a proposal rather than as a bare fact because it is still argued: industry wants it narrowed to exclude gas, and environment groups want it extended to large-scale land clearing. Its status, enacted and in force, is part of the context, not the argument.
contextDisagreement: Supporters say the exclusion is the strongest sense in which the reforms do not trade protection for speed. Opponents in industry say it treats a gas peaker the same as a coal mine and will slow the firming capacity the transition needs. Some environment groups say it does not go far enough.

otherClaim.title: The 2025 overhaul of national environment law will deliver faster approvals without weakening protection

claimItself.title: The 2025 overhaul of national environment law will deliver faster approvals without weakening protection
claimItself.oneLiner: The reforms have passed. Whether they do both of the things promised is the question as they roll out through 2026.
claimItself.body: The Environment Protection Reform Act passed on 28 November 2025 after a Labor–Greens deal, creating a National Environmental Protection Agency, national environmental standards, a streamlined assessment pathway and a ministerial national-interest exemption. Fossil fuel projects are excluded from the fast track and the exemption. The EPA began on 1 July 2026; the faster assessment provisions commence by 1 December 2026.

ownArguments.text: The reforms leave the minister, not the national environmental standards, as the final decision-maker for high-impact projects

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: The streamlined pathway, bioregional plans and the national-interest exemption could let large-scale land clearing, critical-minerals mines and badly sited renewable projects through with less scrutiny than before

otherClaim.title: Coal and gas projects account for the largest and least reversible impacts the Act assesses, on water, land and climate

claimItself.title: Coal and gas projects account for the largest and least reversible impacts the Act assesses, on water, land and climate
claimItself.oneLiner: The reason the exclusion targets these projects first.
claimItself.body: Large coal mines and unconventional gas fields are the projects for which the Act's water trigger was created, and the only class of project whose scope 1 and 2 emissions must now be disclosed. Their footprints, groundwater effects and operating lives are the largest in the assessment system.

otherClaim.title: Keeping gas supply projects in the slowest approval lane conflicts with the government's reliance on new gas for firming and for the reservation scheme

claimItself.title: Keeping gas supply projects in the slowest approval lane conflicts with the government's reliance on new gas for firming and for the reservation scheme
claimItself.oneLiner: The industry's objection to the exclusion, and the point where the energy and environment debates meet.
claimItself.body: The market operator's plan keeps gas-fired generation as firming through the 2030s, and the east-coast reservation scheme depends on new supply coming on. Excluding gas projects from streamlined assessment means the supply the government is counting on faces the longest process in the system.

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: AEMO's Integrated System Plan relies on gas-fired generation to firm renewables through the 2030s and beyond
